x.A: DataSync over the public internet is encrypted and has retries, but 10 TB per day of sensitive data over a shared internet path is less reliable and less consistent than a dedicated link.
x.B: DataSync is built for moving files to S3 with encryption and integrity checks, and Direct Connect gives a private, consistent connection. This is the most reliable and secure way to move 10 TB of JSON files a day.
x.C: DMS migrates databases, not JSON files on a SAN, and the public internet adds reliability risk.
x.D: DMS is the wrong tool because the data is files on a SAN, not a database, even though Direct Connect would give a private path.

x.A: Hosting the API on EC2 means you manage and scale the server, so it has more operational overhead than API Gateway.
x.B: Glue is not an API ingestion endpoint and cannot receive streamed data from an API this way. Source/destination check is also irrelevant here.
x.C: API Gateway is a managed API, Kinesis Data Streams ingests in real time, Lambda transforms the records, and Firehose delivers them to S3. Everything is managed.
x.D: Glue is not a streaming target for API Gateway, so the API cannot send data to it directly.

x.A: Point-in-time recovery keeps only 35 days of continuous backups, so it can't retain data for 7 years.
x.B: AWS Backup creates backup schedules and retention policies for DynamoDB tables, so a 7 year retention is automated with little effort.
x.C: A manual on-demand backup from the console is not automated, and DynamoDB on-demand backups are not stored in a bucket you choose, so lifecycle rules do not apply that way.
x.D: A custom Lambda backup function requires writing and maintaining code, which is more operational work than AWS Backup.

x.A: On-demand capacity mode charges per request and handles sudden unpredictable spikes with no capacity planning. It costs nothing when the table is idle in the mornings.
x.B: A global secondary index adds query flexibility but does not address cost or unpredictable capacity.
x.C: Provisioned capacity with auto scaling reacts too slowly to very fast spikes and still charges for provisioned capacity when idle.
x.D: Provisioned capacity with global tables adds multi-Region replication the company does not need, and it still has the idle cost and spike problem.

x.A: Making an encrypted AMI and its snapshots public exposes them to everyone, which is not secure.
x.B: You share the AMI only with the MSP's account through launchPermission and update the KMS key policy so that account can use the key. Access is limited to one account.
x.C: The key policy must let the partner's account use the existing customer managed key. Trusting a different key owned by the partner does not allow them to decrypt the snapshots.
x.D: Exporting the AMI to S3 is not the supported path for sharing an encrypted AMI and adds needless steps.

x.A: SNS does not store jobs durably for later processing, and CPU usage doesn't reflect the number of waiting jobs.
x.B: An SQS queue holds jobs durably, but scaling on network usage is a poor signal for the number of jobs. It also uses a launch configuration, which is deprecated.
x.C: SQS holds jobs durably and keeps the system loosely coupled. A launch template and an Auto Scaling group that scales on the number of items in the queue adds and removes nodes as needed.
x.D: SNS is not durable storage for jobs, and the number of published messages is not a good scaling signal.

x.A: ACM has no rule feature that publishes a daily custom message to SNS, so this isn't possible.
x.B: An AWS Config rule such as acm-certificate-expiration-check flags certificates that expire within 30 days. EventBridge then sends an SNS alert for the noncompliant resource, with almost no custom code.
x.C: Trusted Advisor does not offer this check for certificates imported into ACM in a form you can alarm on this way.
x.D: A custom EventBridge rule and Lambda could be built, but it needs custom code, and EventBridge alone has no built-in time-to-expiry detection for 30 days ahead like Config's rule does.

x.A: Moving the site to EC2 in us-east-1 does not help European users, and a migration is not possible in a few days.
x.B: A dynamic website cannot be hosted on S3 alone, and replicating buckets does not meet the need to keep the backend in the U.S.
x.C: CloudFront caches content at European edge locations and uses a custom origin for the on-premises servers. It can be set up quickly and the backend stays in the United States.
x.D: Geoproximity routing only decides which endpoint DNS returns, and since the servers are all in the U.S., it does not reduce latency.

x.A: Spot Instances can be interrupted, so they are risky for production, and Reserved Instances are a poor fit for dev and test instances that are stopped part of the day.
x.B: Production runs 24/7 so Reserved Instances give the biggest discount. Dev and test run only part of the day and are stopped, so On-Demand lets you pay only for the hours used.
x.C: Spot blocks are interruption-resistant for a few hours but are not suited to 24/7 production, and Reserved Instances don't suit dev and test.
x.D: On-Demand for production costs more than Reserved Instances for always-on workloads, and Spot blocks are limited in duration.

x.A: S3 Object Lock with Versioning enforces write-once-read-many (WORM) behavior, so documents cannot be modified or deleted after they are stored.
x.B: A lifecycle policy moves or expires objects, which does not stop modification or deletion.
x.C: An ACL set to read-only can be changed by an owner, and versioning alone does not stop a deletion or overwrite being permitted.
x.D: Mounting EFS read-only would stop the application from uploading new documents, and users with write access elsewhere could still change data.

x.A: Secrets Manager stores the credentials securely and supports automatic rotation for RDS. The web servers get access through IAM permissions, so rotating frequently needs no changes to the servers.
x.B: OpsCenter is for managing operational issues and is not a place to store credentials.
x.C: S3 can hold credentials but has no rotation, so the company would build and run that itself.
x.D: Encrypted files on each web server make rotation a manual job across all servers, which is error-prone.

x.A: RDS Proxy pools connections and speeds failover, but it cannot store customer data while the database is unavailable during an upgrade.
x.B: A retry in Lambda is limited by the 15 minute maximum run time, and the data would be lost if the function times out before the upgrade finishes.
x.C: Lambda local storage is temporary and not shared or durable, so data could be lost.
x.D: Writing the data to an SQS FIFO queue stores it durably, and a separate Lambda function stores it into the database when it is available again, so no customer data is lost during an upgrade.

x.A: Requester Pays makes the marketing firm pay for the request and data transfer costs of its own access, so the company's transfer costs stay as low as possible.
x.B: Cross-Region Replication would have the survey company pay for replication and data transfer out, which raises its costs.
x.C: Cross-account access lets the firm read the data, but the bucket owner still pays the data transfer charges.
x.D: Intelligent-Tiering lowers storage costs for changing access and does not reduce transfer charges. Syncing the bucket makes the company pay the transfer.

x.A: Versioning keeps previous object versions and MFA Delete requires a second factor to permanently delete versions, which guards against accidental deletion.
x.B: MFA on IAM users protects sign-in, but a user with permission can still delete objects by accident once signed in.
x.C: A lifecycle policy applies to bucket objects, not IAM users, and cannot deny actions during audit dates.
x.D: Restricting access to the KMS key would stop auditors from reading the documents and does not prevent deletion.

x.A: Multi-AZ gives failover and a standby that cannot be used for read queries, so it does not take load off the primary.
x.B: A read replica receives replicated data, and pointing the reporting script to it moves the load off the primary database, so development work is no longer slowed down. It takes little effort to set up.
x.C: Asking developers to export manually every day is a manual process that does not fix performance.
x.D: ElastiCache caches repeated queries, but a counting script that runs at random intervals would not benefit much, and it adds code changes.

x.A: An S3 gateway endpoint routes S3 traffic privately from the VPC over the AWS network, so traffic never crosses the internet.
x.B: S3 buckets are not placed in subnets. The bucket is a Regional service, so this isn't a valid configuration.
x.C: Putting the bucket in the same Region does not change the network path, and traffic would still go over the internet.
x.D: A NAT gateway sends traffic out to the internet through an internet gateway, which violates the requirement.

x.A: A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 gives the instances private access to S3 without using the internet.
x.B: Making the objects public exposes sensitive data to everyone, which is the opposite of secure access.
x.C: A bucket policy that limits access to the VPC or VPC endpoint ensures only the application tier can reach the sensitive data.
x.D: Copying long-term IAM credentials onto instances is insecure. An IAM role should be used instead.
x.E: A NAT instance sends traffic out to the internet and adds management work, which does not meet the secure private access goal.

x.A: Aurora with Multi-AZ replicas helps production, but a mysqldump backup and restore is slow, and it loads the production database during the export.
x.B: Aurora with replicas handles heavy reads and gives high availability. Aurora cloning creates the staging database on demand quickly, without affecting production performance.
x.C: The Multi-AZ standby of RDS cannot be used for read or staging traffic, and it is for failover only.
x.D: RDS read replicas help reads, but a mysqldump backup and restore still takes a long time and loads the production database.

x.A: EMR is for big data clusters and is overkill for simple one-time transformations on small files. It also adds cluster management.
x.B: EC2 instances must be scaled up and down, and they are idle on days with no uploads, so it has more operational overhead.
x.C: S3 notifications to SQS and a Lambda function are serverless and scale with the number of files, so files are processed quickly and there are no servers to run on quiet days. DynamoDB stores the JSON.
x.D: EventBridge to Kinesis Data Streams adds streaming infrastructure that is not needed, and Aurora is more costly to run for a variable workload.

x.A: Multi-AZ keeps a standby for failover, and the standby doesn't serve traffic, so it does not separate reads from writes.
x.B: The secondary in a Multi-AZ deployment isn't readable. Standby instances are for failover only.
x.C: Read replicas with half the compute and storage could lag behind or struggle under the read load, so performance could stay poor.
x.D: Read replicas with the same compute and storage as the source can handle the read traffic well, which separates reads from writes quickly.

x.A: The policy applies only to us-east-1, so users cannot terminate instances in any other Region.
x.B: The IP address condition is about the user's source address, not the IP address of the EC2 instance.
x.C: The policy allows ec2:TerminateInstances in the us-east-1 Region only when the user's source IP is in the allowed 10.100.100.0/24 range, which includes 10.100.100.254.
x.D: The statement is an Allow, not a Deny, so users from that source IP can terminate instances.

x.A: EFS uses NFS and does not support Windows SMB shares or Active Directory domain authentication in this way.
x.B: A file gateway is meant for hybrid access to S3 and is not a highly available Windows shared file system for SharePoint.
x.C: S3 is object storage, and mounting a bucket as a Windows volume is not supported natively for shared file storage.
x.D: FSx for Windows File Server provides fully managed SMB shares, is highly available with Multi-AZ, and integrates with Active Directory for access control.

x.A: Long polling reduces empty responses and cost but does not stop a message from being delivered again.
x.B: FIFO with a deduplication ID only removes duplicates sent to the queue, not repeated deliveries caused by the visibility timeout, and it means more changes.
x.C: If the visibility timeout is shorter than the function timeout plus the batch window, the message becomes visible again and invokes Lambda a second time. Raising it above that total stops repeated processing.
x.D: Deleting the message before processing risks losing the message if the function fails, and it requires code changes.

x.A: A Storage Gateway file gateway supports NFS and SMB, not Lustre clients.
x.B: A Windows file share on EC2 is not Lustre and is not fully managed.
x.C: EFS is an NFS file system and cannot be configured to support Lustre.
x.D: FSx for Lustre is a fully managed Lustre file system that Lustre clients can use.

x.A: Secrets Manager stores secrets, but manually updating certificates adds work and it does not provide near-real-time encrypt and decrypt operations.
x.B: A custom Lambda function with a Python crypto library means writing and maintaining the encryption code, and storing the function in S3 doesn't make it secure.
x.C: A KMS customer managed key lets the EC2 role encrypt and decrypt in near real time with fine-grained control, and S3 provides highly available storage for the encrypted data.
x.D: KMS works, but EBS is tied to one AZ and one instance, so it is less highly available than S3.
